newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria bourse regulator wants freer bond market.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria bourse regulator wants freer bond market.

text.p: Nigeria's Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Thursday called for a liberalisation of the bond market to increase activity.
In its annual report, the SEC's director general said a market-driven bond pricing system was required to activate the infrequently traded sector.

"An active bond market, particularly in an era of economic and capital market deregulation, is vital to the development of the industrial sector as well as commercialised parastatals," the report said.
Analysts blamed low bond volume on uncompetitive returns.
Current coupon rates for gilts are between 6.0 percent and 12.5 percent, payable every six months, while the band for industrial loans is between 9.0 percent and 28.0 percent.
"It is a bit difficult to invest in instruments whose coupon rates we know to be below (the) inflation rate," said Hamilton Hammer securities analyst Bayo Adeniji.
Inflation dropped to 31 percent in May from 89 percent a year earlier and is seen falling further.
Bank rates are officially capped at 21 percent.
But 91-day treasury bills have a coupon rate of 12 percent while the minimum rediscount rate is 13.5 percent.
The best performers recently have been equities, which have undoubtedly benefitted from the strictures applied to government paper and bank deposits.
Adeniji said falling inflation could be responsible for a sudden spurt in gilt activity on Tuesday when three deals worth 64.5 million naira were struck in government development stocks.
In 1995, traded debt securities accounted for only 2.9 percent of market capitalisation on the Nigerian Stock Exchange.

In the SEC's annual report, director-general George Akamiokhor said state-owned electricity and telecoms utilities, as well as state and local governments, should be encouraged to raise funds from the capital market through bond issues.
However, that is currently extremely difficult because prior approval from the minister of finance is required before states can borrow from the capital market.
But Hayford Alile, chief executive of the stock exchange, said on Tuesday a committee had been set up to recommend ways to reactivate the gilt and bond markets.
